title: Al-Qurtubi's commentary
hookLine: the Andalusian commentator focused on law
tomorrow: two good options, one choice. how do you weigh it?

lines: THE VERSE: WASH, UP TO THE ELBOWS.
cards: Every restaurant restroom has the sign: employees must wash hands. Simple, until somebody asks: how long, up to where, does a quick rinse count?
The Qur'an has a hand-washing verse too: "O ye who believe! When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows." It goes on: wipe your heads, wash your feet to the ankles.
That's the washing before prayer, wudu. Short and clear. Then a scholar from Cordoba, in Muslim Spain, sat down with it, and found a page of law inside.

teach.b: That scholar is al-Qurtubi, and his commentary is called the Collection of the Qur'an's Rulings. He reads verses for what they ask people to do, and he asks the questions a body asks at the sink.

teach.h: UP TO, OR INCLUDING, THE ELBOWS?
teach.b: Does "up to the elbows" include the elbows, or stop just short? Does the washing need an intention behind it, or is wet enough? How much of the head is wiped?

teach.h: WHOLE HEAD OR PART: SCHOOLS DIFFER.
teach.b: Here the schools of law split: Imam Malik, whose school al-Qurtubi followed, says the whole head; al-Shafi'i says part of it is enough. Al-Qurtubi gives his own school's view and lays out the others with their reasons.
Even the feet carry a question.
The Arabic has two recognized readings at that word, and they point different ways: Sunni schools wash the feet; Shia jurists wipe them. One vowel, two practices, each with its own careful reasoning.
Here's the thing worth repeating tonight: one short verse about washing up holds a page of law, and scholars who differ over it are each trying to obey it.
Law in the verses, all the way down to the elbow.

how: Muslims make wudu before prayer, washing the face, the hands and arms to the elbows, wiping the head and washing (or, for Shia Muslims, wiping) the feet; students of Islamic law read al-Qurtubi for how the verses yield rulings.

o: a history of the mosques of Muslim Spain
a Qur'an commentary from Cordoba focused on its rulings
a book of hand-washing customs from many lands

games.q: the law in one verse — tap the pairs.
p: part of the head is enough

s: a short, clear verse always means one simple rule
al-Qurtubi finds a page of questions in one verse about washing.
al-Qurtubi gives his own school's view and lays out the others
Malik's view, and al-Shafi'i's, each with its reasons.
Muslims all agree on how wudu treats the head and feet
the schools differ on the head; Sunni and Shia practice differ on the feet.

games.q: your Shia friend wipes her feet in wudu instead of washing them. a Sunni classmate says she's doing it wrong. what fits al-Qurtubi's way of reading?
o: she's wrong; the verse plainly says wash and nothing else.
the Arabic has two readings there; Sunnis wash, Shia jurists wipe.
it doesn't matter much; the feet aren't really part of wudu.
games.why: one word, two recognized readings, two practices, each reasoned from the verse. law in the verses, read with care.

practice: If there's water near you, wash your hands slowly, up to the wrists or to the elbows, feeling the water at each part. If not, run one palm slowly over the back of the other hand and up the forearm, as if washing.
Let each part get your full attention, one at a time, as the verse names them.

wordCard.voice: Al-Qurtubi's commentary: the Collection of the Qur'an's Rulings, by a scholar of Cordoba who read the verses for the law inside them.

orig.note: Arabic: ahkam, rulings; the word in the name of al-Qurtubi's commentary.

carryVoice: What stays: law in the verses, down to where the water stops. Commentators, three of six.

sources.q: O ye who believe! When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows

sources.ref: al-Qurtubi, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an, on 5:6 (the elbows, intention, wiping the head in Malik's and al-Shafi'i's schools, the two readings at 'your feet')
